paragraphs: I'm Kiran — a backend and AI engineer based in Bangalore, India (open to relocate and remote). I engineer the systems that sit quietly underneath products, handling scale, concurrency, and reliability.

Having built AI-powered health platforms serving 5M+ users at Ultrahuman, multi-tenant B2B architectures at Pencil, and developer tooling at KeyValue, I focus on the seam of scale, performance, and craft.

My work centers on Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, autonomous agent workflows, event-driven microservices, high-throughput database schemas, and developer SDKs. I'm actively seeking full-time and remote backend / AI engineering opportunities.

chapters.title: Case
chapters.summary: Backend Engineer on a 16-person engineering team; 3-person health reporting group owning the report generation pipeline.
chapters.body: Ultrahuman builds metabolic and longevity hardware (including the Ring AIR and Blood Vision) trusted by over 5M+ users worldwide. Within a 16-person team, I worked in a 3-person health reporting group (a lead and two engineers) owning the AI report-generation pipeline, alongside contributing to on-device Kotlin Multiplatform vital computation, a separate platform-wide app and website localization system, and behavioral cross-product recommendations.
points: Team & Scope: 16-person core engineering team; 3-person health reporting group (lead + 2 engineers) owning the end-to-end report generation pipeline.
Scale: Backend and on-device systems serving a global platform of 5M+ active users.
Core Systems: AI health report-generation pipeline, on-device KMP vital computation, separate platform-wide app & website localization system, and cross-product recommendation engine.

chapters.title: Problem
chapters.summary: Three distinct architectural bottlenecks spanning clinical reporting, cloud vital latency, and global app/website localization.

subsections.title: Fragmented Asynchronous Diagnostics & Doctor-in-the-Loop Validation
subsections.body: Health assessments span 10–15 disparate testing stations (DEXA, VO₂ max, blood biomarkers, gut microbiome). Results arrive asynchronously via APIs, PDFs, or delayed lab feeds arriving days later. Autonomous LLMs cannot be treated as final medical authority without qualified clinician review and granular section-level regeneration.
points: Heterogeneous inputs: REST APIs, PDF extracts, and asynchronous external laboratory feeds arriving days apart.
Clinical accuracy & safety: LLM recommendations require doctor review and validation before reaching users.
Regeneration cost: Editing a single recommendation previously required manually re-running the entire 15–20 page document.

subsections.title: Cloud Batch Queue Latency & Network Dependency for Vital Scores
subsections.body: Core sleep, recovery, and vital sign calculations were processed centrally on backend Ruby servers in scheduled batch jobs across users, introducing multi-second delays and failing when wearers lacked internet access.
points: High latency: Ring wearers woke up to delayed scores waiting for backend queue execution.
Network vulnerability: 0% offline execution; vitals could not be computed without cloud roundtrips.
Parity risk: Migrating vital calculations to device risked mathematical divergence from historical server baselines.

subsections.title: CJK Translation Nuance & Terminology Drift Across Global Apps & Web
subsections.body: A separate standalone translation workflow powered user-facing localization across the entire Ultrahuman mobile apps and website. Standard LLM translation failed on Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK) due to context nuances, terminology drift, and trademark transliteration.
points: Context-dependent phrasing: CJK grammar requires deep domain context rather than verbatim literal translation.
Brand integrity: Lack of glossary constraints caused inconsistent transliteration of proprietary terms.
Repetitive overhead: Lack of prompt caching resulted in high token costs and latency on recurring system context.

chapters.title: Goal
chapters.summary: Target engineering objectives mapped directly to each of the three problem statements.

subsections.title: Dynamic Asynchronous Pipeline & Granular Clinician Regeneration
subsections.body: Build an asynchronous pipeline that dynamically triggers as prerequisite lab results arrive, producing 15–20 page reports with a doctor review loop allowing single-section regeneration.
points: Dynamic station DAG: Handle asynchronous data arrival without blocking or stalling reporting flows.
Human-in-the-loop: Generate → Review → Comment → Regenerate → Approve workflow for doctors.
Scoped section diffing: Regenerate only commented sections (e.g., diet plan) in seconds.

subsections.title: 100% On-Device Vital Computation with Strict Parity
subsections.body: Port sleep and recovery algorithms to Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) running locally on-device, cutting latency by ~80% while proving 99–100% parity against server baselines.
points: Immediate local computation: Remove cloud batch processing dependency entirely.
100% offline execution: Enable users to compute recovery and vitals anywhere without connectivity.
Empirical validation: Prove parity across diverse device architectures with real ring wearer datasets.

subsections.title: High-Fidelity CJK App & Website Localization with Prompt Caching
subsections.body: Upgrade the platform-wide translation pipeline for CJK languages using curated domain glossaries, split contextual passes, and prompt caching to exceed 90% quality.
points: Glossary enforcement: Maintain exact trademark transliterations and medical terminology.
Split-translation architecture: Contextual analysis followed by nuanced script generation.
Prompt caching: Minimize latency and token cost on recurring app and website translation prompts.

chapters.title: Approach
chapters.summary: Three dedicated architectural implementations addressing reporting, on-device execution, and global platform localization.

subsections.title: Dynamic Report Generation Pipeline & Clinician-in-the-Loop Loop
subsections.body: Owned the end-to-end report generation pipeline within the 3-person reporting group. Built dynamic DAG compilation that triggers as prerequisite stations arrive, coupled with a clinician feedback loop that regenerates specific sections based on doctor comments without re-running the full document.
points: Dynamic Ingestion DAG: Reconciles REST APIs and extracted lab PDFs into a unified biomarker schema.
Predefined Guidance Rules: Bound LLM reasoning to research-backed clinical rules and prompt constraints.
Targeted Section Regeneration: Doctors annotate specific blocks, triggering focused prompt regeneration that leaves the rest of the 15–20 page report intact.

subsections.title: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) On-Device Computation Port
subsections.body: Contributed to shifting health computation from server background queues to on-device execution. Ported vital algorithms from Ruby to Kotlin Multiplatform and validated parity against real ring wearers.
points: Ruby to KMP Migration: Rewrote computation pipelines in shared Kotlin Multiplatform running natively on device.
Parity Test Suite: Built validation harness comparing server and device outputs against real ring wearer biometrics, proving 99–100% mathematical parity.
Latency Elimination: Reduced computation latency by ~80% and unlocked instant offline vital computation.

subsections.title: Separate Platform-Wide App & Website Localization Pipeline
subsections.body: Independent of health reporting, engineered a dedicated LLM translation flow powering user-facing localization across the entire Ultrahuman mobile applications and marketing web platform.
points: Curated Glossary Injection: Injected strict domain glossaries and trademark preservation rules for CJK scripts.
Split-Translation Passes: Divided translation into context analysis and localized generation for nuanced grammar.
Prompt Caching: Cached repetitive system instructions and contextual glossaries, dramatically slashing latency and token costs.

subsections.title: Behavioral Cohort Cross-Product Recommendation Engine
subsections.body: Constructed an automated behavioral recommendation engine evaluating real-time user signals into cohorts (e.g., UltrahumanX, cycle/ovulation tracking, cardio capabilities) for contextual discovery.
points: Behavioral Cohorting: Segmented users by activity patterns rather than broadcasting static promotional banners.
Proven Conversion: Generated 8,000+ cross-product conversions within two months of deployment.

chapters.title: Outcome
chapters.summary: 80% latency reduction, 99–100% parity, 8,000+ conversions in 60 days, and 93% Chinese translation quality across 5M+ users.

table.impact: 99–100% parity validated with real ring wearers

chapters.title: Learning
chapters.summary: Key technical takeaways on production LLM architecture, clinician-in-the-loop workflows, and edge computing.

takeaways.title: AI systems need structured workflows, not just prompts
takeaways.body: Production LLM applications are 90% ingestion, normalization, deterministic validation, and scoped regeneration rails. The model is merely one execution step in a resilient pipeline.

takeaways.title: Human review as a core product primitive
takeaways.body: In high-stakes health domains, total autonomy is an antipattern. Designing granular review, diffing, and single-section regeneration gives clinicians leverage without compromising medical accuracy.

takeaways.title: Architect for real-world asynchronous data
takeaways.body: Real-world medical data never arrives cleanly synchronized. Decoupling station dependencies prevents whole-system stalls when external lab feeds lag by days.

takeaways.title: Edge vs. cloud changes the interaction paradigm
takeaways.body: Migrating computation from background batch queues to on-device KMP isn't just an optimization; it transforms user experience from waiting for background jobs to instantaneous feedback.

chapters.title: Case
chapters.summary: Backend Engineer in a 4-person engineering team with a technical lead at KeyValue Software Systems building Siren's AI-native layer.
chapters.body: Siren is a developer communication platform that helps engineering teams design and deliver notifications across email, SMS, push notifications, and chat. Working as part of a four-person engineering group with a technical lead, my focus was making Siren AI-native by exposing its communication capabilities to AI agents through a reusable Agent Toolkit and a standardized Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.
points: Team & Scope: 4-person engineering group with a technical lead owning the AI-agent integration layer.
Primary Ownership: Framework adoption, tool schema conversion, OpenAI/LangChain/CrewAI compatible tools, MCP tool implementations, agent integrations, documentation, and examples.
Collaborative Delivery: Automated packaging and CI/CD publishing workflows were established by another team engineer.
Core Objective: Let developers instruct AI agents on what they want to communicate via natural language intent, rather than writing boilerplate integration code for every notification channel.

chapters.title: Problem
chapters.summary: Three distinct engineering challenges: rigid imperative SDK wiring, fragmented agent framework interfaces, and rapidly shifting ecosystem specifications.

subsections.title: Rigid API/SDK Wiring vs. Intent-Driven Communication
subsections.body: Traditional notification integrations forced developers to write imperative boilerplate (Application → SDK → Notification API → Email/SMS/Push), manually selecting operations, constructing request payloads, and writing routing logic. As AI agents emerged, developers needed an intent-based model where an agent could execute high-level instructions ('Send an email to the new user welcoming them') without bespoke code for each trigger.
points: Imperative integration friction: Developers spent hours writing plumbing code for standard notification triggers.
Lack of semantic understanding: APIs could not interpret natural language instructions directly.
High barrier for AI agents: Existing endpoints lacked schemas that LLMs could reason about or call safely.

subsections.title: Incompatible Tool Conventions Across Agent Ecosystems
subsections.body: Different agent frameworks (OpenAI Function Calling, LangChain, CrewAI) expected tools and schemas to be defined, validated, and executed with completely different signatures and parameter structures. Forcing developers to hand-roll custom adapters for every Siren operation in each framework created severe integration fragmentation.
points: Schema incompatibility: OpenAI JSON schemas, LangChain StructuredTools, and CrewAI tools require divergent formats.
Dual-language barrier: Enterprise stacks required idiomatic tooling across both TypeScript/Node.js and Python ecosystems.
Maintenance overhead: Supporting multiple frameworks without a shared core layer led to duplicated logic and brittle glue code.

subsections.title: Building Against Rapidly Evolving Specifications & Standards
subsections.body: AI agent tooling and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) were in their earliest releases when development began. Upstream specifications, client conventions, and library APIs were shifting continuously without established industry best practices, making stability and future-proof design a strict engineering constraint.
points: Unstable upstream APIs: Framework tool interfaces and protocol drafts underwent frequent breaking changes.
Absence of battle-tested patterns: Integration conventions had to be architected from scratch through empirical testing against agent workflows.
Compatibility pressure: Integrations had to remain reliable for developers while the underlying standards were actively maturing.

chapters.title: Goal
chapters.summary: Target engineering objectives mapped directly to developer experience, cross-framework compatibility, and resilient MCP standardization.

subsections.title: Natural Language Intent as the Integration Layer
subsections.body: Shift Siren's primary interaction model from purely API-oriented to intent-oriented, enabling agents to parse natural-language instructions, determine the correct notification operation, and construct payloads while preserving developer control over explicit templates.
points: Intent resolution: Enable agents to trigger complex notifications from simple prompt instructions.
Preserve developer control: Allow explicit templates, content overrides, and parameter constraints when needed.
Effort reduction: Cut developer integration overhead by ~75% for AI-driven communication workflows.

subsections.title: Unified Agent Toolkit & Native Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server
subsections.body: Build a single reusable abstraction layer over Siren's capabilities and expose it via both a cross-framework Agent Toolkit (TypeScript & Python) and a standalone MCP server executable via npx.
points: Framework agnostic: Native compatibility with OpenAI, LangChain, CrewAI, and custom agent swarms.
Standard protocol: Support standardized tool discovery and invocation via the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
Dual-language SDKs: Provide idiomatic @trysiren/agent-toolkit (npm) and siren-agent-toolkit (PyPI) packages.

subsections.title: Resilient Adapter Architecture for Rapidly Shifting Specs
subsections.body: Design clean decoupled boundaries between internal Siren operations and external agent frameworks, insulating application developers from upstream protocol churn and specification updates.
points: Decoupled tool schemas: Isolate core platform capabilities from framework-specific serialization formats.
Continuous compatibility: Maintain stable developer DX across iterative agent framework releases.
Self-documenting interfaces: Provide comprehensive documentation, quickstarts, and sample agent workflows.

chapters.title: Approach
chapters.summary: Architecture bridging existing Siren platform capabilities with agent frameworks and MCP servers through reusable tool schemas.

subsections.title: Tool Schema Conversion & Multi-Framework Agent Toolkit
subsections.body: Mapped Siren's existing platform operations (messaging, templates, users, workflows) into structured agent-callable tools. Built a unified core abstraction that dynamically converts schemas into framework-specific signatures for OpenAI Function Calling, LangChain StructuredTools, and CrewAI across TypeScript (@trysiren/agent-toolkit) and Python (siren-agent-toolkit).
points: Semantic tool definitions: Authored descriptive schemas and parameters so LLMs understand tool purpose reliably.
Multi-framework adapters: Provided drop-in compatibility across OpenAI, LangChain, and CrewAI without vendor lock-in.
Dual-stack distribution: Maintained parity across TypeScript/Node.js and Python implementations.

subsections.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server Implementation
subsections.body: Architected a dedicated MCP server package (@trysiren/mcp) implementing the standardized Model Context Protocol over JSON-RPC. Allows Claude desktop, cursor agents, and external agent runtimes to dynamically discover and invoke Siren tools directly via npx (@trysiren/mcp) without custom integration code.
points: Standard tool discovery: Exposed Siren communication tools through the universal MCP specification.
Zero-install execution: Supported direct execution via npx -y @trysiren/mcp for frictionless local and server workflows.
Granular capability exposure: Enabled agents to inspect available templates and send single or batch dispatches safely.

subsections.title: Decoupled Adapter Boundaries Under Changing Standards
subsections.body: Treated rapid ecosystem evolution as a core engineering constraint. Designed clear abstraction barriers between raw Siren REST endpoints and external agent schemas, allowing our team to absorb upstream specification changes (such as MCP draft updates and framework method renames) without breaking end-developer applications.
points: Defensive abstraction layers: Shielded application developers from frequent upstream API and spec shifts.
Empirical agent validation: Tested tool invocations against live agent runs to detect prompt regression early.
Ecosystem adaptability: Kept public integration patterns stable even as underlying packages evolved.

subsections.title: Public Documentation, Examples & Technical Strategy
subsections.body: Co-authored public technical documentation, implementation quickstarts, and architectural guides on how to make existing B2B products AI-native. Documented integration patterns for multi-agent swarms (CrewAI) and autonomous workflows.
points: Official documentation: Authored comprehensive setup guides for Agent Toolkit and MCP server.
Real-world examples: Built end-to-end agent workflow demos for welcome emails and transactional alerts.
Technical strategy publication: Published technical article on KeyValue's engineering blog regarding AI-native product transitions.

chapters.title: Learning
chapters.summary: Key technical lessons on making existing platforms AI-native, tool schema engineering, and early-ecosystem adaptability.

takeaways.title: AI-native doesn't mean rebuilding the product
takeaways.body: Siren already had robust notification delivery capabilities. The challenge was building an agent-facing discovery and execution layer over existing capabilities rather than duplicating underlying infrastructure.

takeaways.title: Tool design matters as much as model quality
takeaways.body: An AI agent can only reliably use a capability if the tool interface is understandable. Designing explicit schemas, clear parameter constraints, and intuitive descriptions is critical for reliable agent execution.

takeaways.title: Early ecosystems require adaptability as an architecture feature
takeaways.body: Working with rapidly evolving agent frameworks and MCP specifications meant engineering wasn't simply following established documentation. Decoupled adapter layers allowed us to maintain a stable developer experience while the underlying ecosystem matured.

faqs: Do you both design and build websites?
Yes. I handle the whole thing, design and development, with one set of hands. My experience spans full-stack products, backend platforms, and the interfaces that connect people to them.
Where are you based, and do you work remotely?
I'm based in Bangalore, India (open to relocate and remote) and work with teams across the world.
What technologies do you build with?

I work mostly with Ruby on Rails, TypeScript, Node.js, Python, FastAPI, React, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS, and MCP. I choose the tools around the problem rather than forcing every product into one stack.
Can you build an online store or e-commerce site?
Yes. I've built service architectures and inventory and order-processing workflows for e-commerce products, with a focus on reliable backend systems and integrations.
How much does a website cost?

It depends entirely on what you need. I work across a wide range of budgets, from smaller sites through to large, complex builds. Tell me what you have in mind and I'll scope it and give you a clear, fixed quote.
How long does a project take?
Most sites take from a few weeks to a couple of months, depending on scope, content readiness and how many rounds of feedback we go through. I'll give you a realistic timeline up front.
Can you redesign or rebuild my existing website?

Yes. A lot of my work is refreshing tired sites that no longer reflect the quality of the business, including migrations from older WordPress builds, with care taken to keep your SEO and rankings intact.
Do you offer ongoing support after launch?
Yes. I offer ongoing support and retainer agreements to keep your site updated, secure and performing after launch and as your business scales.

freelance.title: Client Services & Web Consulting
freelance.headline: Web Design, Development & Client Consulting
freelance.subline: For founders, agencies, and businesses looking for custom web design, WordPress migrations, digital product architecture, and project scoping.
faqs: Do you both design and build websites?
Yes. I handle the whole thing, design and development, with one set of hands. My experience spans full-stack products, backend platforms, and the interfaces that connect people to them.
Where are you based, and do you work remotely?
I'm based in Bangalore, India (open to relocate and remote) and work with teams across the world.
What technologies do you build with?

I work mostly with Ruby on Rails, TypeScript, Node.js, Python, FastAPI, React, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS, and MCP. I choose the tools around the problem rather than forcing every product into one stack.
Can you build an online store or e-commerce site?
Yes. I've built service architectures and inventory and order-processing workflows for e-commerce products, with a focus on reliable backend systems and integrations.
How much does a website cost?

It depends entirely on what you need. I work across a wide range of budgets, from smaller sites through to large, complex builds. Tell me what you have in mind and I'll scope it and give you a clear, fixed quote.
How long does a project take?
Most sites take from a few weeks to a couple of months, depending on scope, content readiness and how many rounds of feedback we go through. I'll give you a realistic timeline up front.
Can you redesign or rebuild my existing website?

Yes. A lot of my work is refreshing tired sites that no longer reflect the quality of the business, including migrations from older WordPress builds, with care taken to keep your SEO and rankings intact.
Do you offer ongoing support after launch?
Yes. I offer ongoing support and retainer agreements to keep your site updated, secure and performing after launch and as your business scales.
